Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q26.text: Structurally imbalanced, honestly -- the supervisor-student relationship concentrates power in ways that are genuinely hard to challenge, and advancement depends more on who you know than what you produce. I think thats baked in by design, not accident.

Q16.text: The networking side of things, honestly -- access to opportunities depends almost entirely on who introduces you to whom, usually through your supervisor. If they're not well-connected or dont actively advocate for you, you're at a structural disadvantage before you've even submitted.

Q55.text: How much the supervisor's network shapes your actual trajectory -- not just research quality, but introductions, recommendations, job prospects. I chose based on research fit and didnt think to assess connectivity, which turned out to be a costly omission.

Q41.text: Industry R&D -- I'd rather work somewhere the incentive structures are a bit more transparent, and advancement isn't contingent on one person's goodwill.

Q60.text: Appreciate that surveys like this exist -- these concerns rarely surface through official channels, and when they do they're often depersonalised into aggregate statistics. the supervisor dynamic is genuinely hard to reform from within, but documenting it matters.

Q17.text: The intellectual exchange with peers, honestly -- that part's been genuinely stimulating. Everything else is more complicated.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system works on networking and knowing people, including the publication system. The fact that the student has to obtain a recommendation from the supervisor for any post-doctoral position is an example feature of a system that is stuck in the old era. And the student is extremely lucky if the supervisor is friendly, knowledgeable and most importantly, has the welfare of the student and their career as one of his/her priorities. I was unlucky. But, in my opinion, it is the fault of the system to have such a highly skewed power structure. The student is guaranteed to be exploited, by design.

Q26.text: Broken, honestly. I've been around academia long enough -- this is my second PhD, different field -- to know the meritocracy thing is pretty much a myth. People advance because they know the right people or they're in the right lab, not because their work is actually the best. The politics are exhausting and the nepotism is real, its kind of absurd when you see it play out up close. The actual science though, the questions I get to work on, still feel worth it to me. But the institution itself has been a pretty consistent disappointment

Q16.text: The age thing is something I didn't anticipate being such a factor. I came back for a second doctorate knowing it was a risk, but the assumption that anyone over 40 applying for positions is somehow a liability -- that's real and nobody talks about it openly. And the funding landscape has gotten genuinely worse since I started, grant cycles feel more competitive and the criteria more arbitrary. I'm not panicking but its something that sits in the back of my mind more than I expected it to

Q55.text: How much the relationships matter over the actual work. I came in both times genuinely believing that the quality of the research would be the main currency, and its just not. Who your advisor knows, whether you're in the right political camp within your department -- that stuff shapes your trajectory more than your publications do, and nobody tells you that going in. I wish someone had just been upfront about it instead of letting me learn it the hard way.

Q41.text: Community college or four-year teaching, honestly. I care about teaching more than I do about climbing the research ladder at some R1 where the game is mostly about grant money and departmental politics. I've seen what that looks like and its not where I want to put my energy. Teaching at a smaller institution, actually connecting with students -- that still feels meaningful to me even if the pay isn't going to be great

Q60.text: Yeah, I'd just say that surveys like this are actually useful, and I hope someone reads the responses carefully rather than just running them through a rubric and calling it done. The things that erode a PhD experience -- the petty politics, the arbitrary gatekeeping, the way the system quietly punishes people who don't fit the expected profile -- those are structural and they don't show up in retention statistics. I came into this second doctorate with clear eyes and I still got surprised by some of it. so I appreciate having a place to put that on the record, even if nothing changes.

Q17.text: The actual research, no question. Getting to spend time on questions that genuinely interest me -- the biology, the design of experiments, figuring out what the data is actually telling you -- that part still feels like a privilege, even on the hard days. And there's a kind of intellectual freedom in the PhD that I know I won't have the same way in a teaching role, so I try to appreciate it while its here. Honestly the work itself is what keeps me from walking away from the whole enterprise when the institutional stuff gets to be too much

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

Q26.text: It's genuinely intellectually stimulating, but the economic model -- where universities rely on cheap grad student labour while dangling a career path that statistically won't pan out for most of us -- is kind of hard to ignore the longer you're in it. I'd say the system is set up to benefit from our passion more than it's set up to sustain us.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, honestly — I don't think I anticipated how isolating the work would be, or how much the financial stress would compound that. It's hard to feel fully present in the research when you're running the numbers on whether you can afford rent.

Q55.text: How non-linear the funding landscape is — I think I came in with a perceived notion that if you were good enough and worked hard enough, the path would open up, and that's just not how it works. Knowing earlier that career outcomes are largely structural rather than meritocratic would have reframed a lot of my early anxiety.

Q41.text: Industry research or biotech/pharma -- I'd say the appeal of actually seeing work translated into something real, and the frankly better compensation, outweighs whatever pull academia still has for me. I'm also keeping an eye on business-side roles in those sectors, rn the research career path just doesn't feel economically viable.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this are valuable — there's a lot of anecdotal conversation about PhD conditions but not a lot of systematic data, so I hope the responses here actually feed into something actionable. The financial sustainability piece especially feels underexamined relative to how much it shapes the experience day to day.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual autonomy is hard to beat — being able to follow a question wherever it leads, even when (especially when) it contradicts what you expected to find. and the people, tbh. Being surrounded by others who are genuinely obsessed with their corner of the world makes even the harder stretches feel worthwhile.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's not perfect, but I've failed to think of a viable alternative beyond "have the government put a lot more money into it so that trainees can get paid better (to lead a better quality of life with less stress and thus do better work, of course) and so that there are more opportunities to have independent research programs after postdoc"... I'd say we're quite privileged to be able to do this work, but it's highly competitive and uncertain, which makes it seem less attractive for people like myself who come from non-wealthy backgrounds.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

So financial stress is huge, and is pushing me towards exploring and seriously considering non-academic/non-research career path options.

Q26.text: The academic system strikes me as simultaneously brilliant and deeply parochial — a world that produces extraordinary knowledge yet remains, honestly, strangely reluctant to examine its own structural assumptions. Coming in at this life stage I see the meritocracy mythology more clearly than I might have at 28. Reform is overdue, though not hopeless.

Q16.text: The impostor syndrome is real, honestly, if somewhat expected — I wonder occasionally whether my community-facing research agenda will find institutional traction, or whether academy's preference for inward-facing scholarship will quietly sideline it. Not a crisis, but a live concern

Q55.text: That the dissertation is less about argument than about demonstrating institutional fluency — learning the unwritten grammar of the field. I wish someone had been frank about that distinction early; it would have saved considerable philosophical confusion.

Q41.text: Pro bono research, honestly — I'm not looking to climb any ladder. I envision something like a research professorship structured around NGO and community partnerships, where the work serves actual human needs rather than citation counts. At this stage of life, meaningful contribution is the metric that matters.

Q60.text: The survey itself is well-constructed — I appreciated that it left room for nuance rather than forcing experience into tidy categories. If I were to suggest one amendment: a question about how respondents situate their research within broader social concerns might surface a dimension that current instruments miss. The PhD, at least for those of us arriving from other fields, is as much a negotiation with institutional culture as it is an intellectual undertaking and I suspect that tension is underexplored in the literature on doctoral experience.

Q17.text: The intellectual permission, honestly — the license to pursue a single question with genuine depth over sustained time. After decades of applied work, having institutional legitimacy for slow, careful thinking is something I hadn't quite anticipated valuing this much. The scholarly community is uneven, but at its best it's genuinely stimulating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: As a late career-changer, I have seen the institutional attitude shift from "sink or swim" indifference to a genuine concern with student success. While this is undoubtedly enlightened self-interest on the part of the academy, it is a good first step. The next challenge is preparing grads for real careers. I notice that the concern with the endless postdoc cycle is gaining traction. A societal change, where science is seen not only as credible, but essential to our survival in every sphere, would help create the right atmosphere for bright new minds to flourish and contribute. Here in the USA, this is a problem at present.

Q26.text: Fragmented, honestly. The relationship between my research center and the university feels like a purely economic arrangement -- not really academic partnership. No coursework, limited administrative support, little sense that the university is actually invested in your development as researcher. But the intellectual environment within the research group itself is genuinely stimulating, and that keeps you going. The system could work better with more real integration between universities and research centers, better guidance for PhD students caught between these two structures.

Q16.text: One thing that does weigh on me is the uncertainty about what comes after. Academic job market in Spain is quite limited, and the path to stable research position feels pretty unclear — there's not much structured career guidance either, which honestly fits with the broader lack of institutional support I already mentioned. And because there's no coursework, you also miss out on building a real peer cohort, so the whole experience can feel quite isolated at times.

Q55.text: How disconnected research center experience really is from the university, and what that means in practice. I wish I'd known to actively seek out peers from early on -- without coursework, that network just doesn't form on its own. The intellectual side was never the problem honestly, but the isolation and the structural uncertainty, those caught me off guard more than I expected

Q41.text: Research, ideally within academia or a public research institution, though I'm realistic about how competitive and limited that path is in Spain. I'm committed to staying in research in some form -- whether that ends up being a postdoc abroad or finding a niche in applied research, I haven't fully decided yet.

Q60.text: Mostly I'd just say that the experience has been genuinely valuable intellectually, even if the structural side has been frustrating. I hope surveys like this lead to some real reflection on how universities engage with affiliated research centers -- the people caught in between those two structures deserve better support than they typically get.

Q17.text: The intellectual work, honestly -- that's what keeps me going. Having the freedom to engage seriously with a complex problem, to read deeply and think without the pace of a coursework schedule, that's genuinely fulfilling. The autonomy can tip into isolation at times, but the depth of engagement you get as researcher is something I don't think I'd find in many other contexts.

Si esto cambiase sería de mucha ayuda para todos los estudiantes de PhD y tendría mucho más sentido el seguir vinculado a una universidad.

Q26.text: The academic system is, tbh, a well-veiled pyramid scheme — PIs compete for grants, and graduate students are the inexpensive instrument through which that competition is waged. The idealism that draws people into research is deliberately cultivated and then quietly exploited.

Q16.text: The psychological toll of pretending it's all normal has concerned me -- the way the culture conditions you to treat exploitation as just "how it is." I've also found the gendered dimensions pretty troubling; comments I witnessed about maternity leave made clear that the system reserves a particular contempt for women who want lives outside the lab.

Q55.text: That your supervisor's incentives are structurally misaligned with your wellbeing -- and that no amount of good faith on your part will change that. I wish I'd evaluated my PI the way you'd evaluate an employer, not a mentor.

Q41.text: Teaching at a small liberal arts college — somewhere the emphasis is on students, not on chasing the next grant cycle. I'm done with the research treadmill, honestly.

Q60.text: I hope this research actually reaches the people designing doctoral programs, not just gets cited in papers no one reads. The problems aren't mysterious -- they're structural and well-documented. what's missing is any institutional will to change them, and I'm not holding my breath.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual work itself -- when I actually get to do it. There are moments in research that still feel like the reason I came here. But those moments get harder to access when most of your energy is going toward managing a difficult PI relationship and performing enthusiasm you don't feel.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's becoming clear to me that the academic system constitutes a well-veiled pyramid scheme.  PIs think that grad school is the same as it was for them, and treat their students accordingly.  This is surprising to me, considering success as a scientist requires one to keep up with changing information.  For some reason, there's a blind spot where grad students are concerned.

Q60.text: My PhD program advertised 4 weeks of time off per year, and a generous maternal leave policy. My PI has also remarked to at least one student that not electing to come back from maternity leave early means you don't care enough about science to be successful.

Q26.text: Honestly, the system works — when it works. My own experience has been genuinely positive: good mentorship, reasonable funding, colleagues who push me to think harder. But I'm acutely aware that's not everyone's reality. The academic pipeline rewards people who already have structural advantages, and that self-reinforcing quality is hard to sit with. Reform isn't just needed, it's overdue — especially around who actually gets to stay and succeed in it.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, honestly. I've been lucky — my workload is manageable and I have good support around me — but I watch colleagues in other departments or other institutions just... burning out quietly. And the culture still treats that as a personal failing rather than a structural one. I don't have a crisis to report, but the ambient awareness that it could go differently under slightly different circumstances is something that sits with me.

Q55.text: Communicate early — with your supervisor, with your peers, with yourself about what you actually need. I assumed things would work out if I just kept my head down and produced, and honestly they did, but I got lucky. the people I've watched struggle most are the ones who waited too long to flag a problem or ask for what they needed. Don't mistake silence for self-sufficiency.

Q41.text: Industry research, ideally at an organization working on something with real social impact — I'm drawn to roles where I can bring technical expertise to questions around equity and access in STEM, whether that's ed-tech, policy-adjacent research, or outreach-focused nonprofit work.

Q60.text:
The thing I keep coming back to is how much environment matters — and how invisible that is to people designing interventions. We talk about "PhD student resilience" as if it's a trait, when so much of it is actually just... circumstance. Good supervisor, funded cohort, department that actually talks to each other. I got that. A lot of people don't, and the system doesn't really account for it.

If anything comes out of surveys like this, I hope it's that — a push to think structurally rather than individually about what makes PhDs survivable, let alone good.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. There's something I didn't fully anticipate — the way a PhD gives you permission to just... sit with a hard problem and not rush toward an answer. And my department has made that feel genuinely collaborative rather than isolating, which I know isn't universal. That combination of autonomy and community is, I think, the thing I'd miss most if I lost it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Experience in academia depends greatly on the department, environment, and university one is attending. If one's department is close-knit and very supportive, the experience is great –– some departments are more helpful when it comes to finding funding, helping with housing, etc. It is especially helpful when everyone in your immediate circle acknowledges just how stressful the academic environment can be. I am lucky that I am in an incredibly supportive environment, and I know this reflects on my positive PhD experience. However, that does not discount the struggles that other people may go through, as there are many times where academia can be a very toxic environment –– "publish or perish" is just one contributor to this. There are many improvements that could be made to the academic system.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system that rewards conformity more than genuine intellectual contribution. Funding structures create perverse incentives -- researchers chase grants rather than interesting questions, and this filters down to PhD students who are expected to deliver outputs that tick institutional boxes. There's also significant gatekeeping along gender and racial lines that people don't talk about openly enough. I came from industry where tbh there was more transparency about how decisions get made; academia dresses its hierarchies in the language of merit, which I find harder to stomach.

Q16.text: Financial sustainability is a real concern -- my stipend barely covers rent in this city, and that creates kind of chronic low-level stress that affects everything else. I'm also increasingly anxious about what comes after; the academic job market is brutal, and I dont want it, but even industry paths for PhDs feel opaque. You're trained for one thing and expected to figure out the rest yourself.

Q55.text: That the PhD is as much a political and social navigation exercise as an intellectual one. Knowing earlier that your supervisor's network, their standing in the field, their willingness to advocate for you -- these matter as much as the quality of your actual work. I spent too long assuming merit would speak for itself.

Q41.text: Research scientist or consultant role in an SME or mid-size company, ideally somewhere the work is applied enough to have real impact but still technically rigorous. Academia isnt on the table for me at this point -- the structural issues I've seen make it hard to imagine building a sustainable career there.

Q60.text: I hope this kind of research actually leads to structural change and isn't just another study that gets published and shelved. The issues I've described -- funding pressure, gatekeeping, the opacity of career pathways -- are well-documented at this point. What's lacking is institutional will to act on them. If anything, I'd encourage researchers to pay closer attention to the experiences of international students specifically; we navigate all of these pressures with additional layer of visa dependency and geographic isolation that compounds everything. But overall, good luck with the project.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Having time to go deep on a problem without someone pulling you out for sprint review or a client call -- that's something industry doesnt offer in the same way. I also value being around people who genuinely care about ideas, even if the institution often works against that energy.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Slow!!! So many hierarchical layers to go through before being able to make any meaningful change to the system. Having worked both in industry and academia, I also think academia is as money-driven as industry. The only difference being where the money is coming from. But a lot of the time it feels that the research is more tailored to get good publications to get good grants than for science's sake. PhD students (UK) are also kept under a regime that makes them students, hence unable to unionise, while getting many hours out of them for a stipend that is frankly insufficient compared to our level of expertise. Also, the higher up you go, the more male and white-dominated the environment becomes. There's only one full female professor in my whole institute, and I have genuinely never met a black PI or professor since starting my PhD.

Q16.text: Going back to my home country's job market (France). I want to live there but I'm unsure of the job prospects. They're nonexistent in academia and I have been away from industry for a little while.

Q26.text: A pyramid scheme dressed up as intellectual pursuit, honestly. You come in idealistic, work insane hours for poverty wages, and the people at the top publish your data under their names. And if you're an immigrant on a visa you can't even leave -- you're trapped by paperwork while your life back home falls apart. The system survives because every new cohort thinks they'll be the exception. They wont.

Q16.text:
My sister's wedding. A family funeral. I missed both because I couldn't risk leaving the country mid-visa-renewal. You can't put a dollar figure on that but it costs something.

And there's basically no real mental health support for international students -- the university counselling waitlist is months long and the counsellors dont understand what it means to have your entire immigration status tied to one supervisor who can dismiss you whenever. That's not anxiety you can breathwork your way out of.

Also my partner is still abroad. We've been long distance for four years now. Every time I think I'm close to finishing something pushes the timeline out. Reagents fail, experiments fail, I fail. and at some point you stop being able to explain to someone who loves you why you're still doing this to yourself.

Q55.text: That the supervisor relationship isn't just professional -- it's total. Your visa, your stipend, your publications, your timeline, all of it runs through one person who has no real accountability. I thought it was a mentorship. It's closer to indentured labour with a power imbalance so steep that "raising concerns" is basically career suicide. Wish someone had said that plainly before I signed anything.

Q41.text: Honestly I don't know anymore. I came in wanting an academic career but that's a lottery with worse odds every year, and I'm not even competitive -- barely any publications, no real network outside my own lab. Industry wants skills I dont have. I've spent years doing experiments that didn't work and writing failed grant sections for my supervisor. I dont know what that translates to outside this building

Q60.text:
Just that I hope someone actually reads these. Not to compile a report that sits in a folder somewhere, but to actually reckon with the fact that there are people in these programs who are not okay -- not in a "needs more wellness workshops" way but in a structural, systemic, nobody-is-accountable way.

I dont expect anything to change. But it felt worth saying it somewhere.

Q17.text:
Genuinely? There are moments -- rare ones -- when an experiment works and the data actually says something. For about ten minutes you remember why you started. Then you have to write it up, fight over authorship, and explain to your supervisor why the figures aren't publication-ready yet. So the enjoyment has a pretty short half-life.

I guess the autonomy, technically. No one tells me when to come in. But that's also because no one cares enough to notice if I dont show up, so I'm not sure it counts.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q16.text: I am far from my family and I cannot go back to them to visit because I only have 1 year visa stamp and no time to renew my visa - usually more than 1.5mo of waiting away from the bench. I will never be in the same country that my family is in because my expertise is not valued there at all (and not valued here so much but I can buy food). Two of my close relatives died and I did not come to say my good byes. My boyfriend is doing PhD in a different country. I hate this.

Q26.text: A system that extracts labor from those most vulnerable to exploitation — early-career researchers with precarious funding and conditional futures — while rewarding absentee supervisors with institutional prestige. The rhetoric of "academic community" papers over what is, in practice, a deeply asymmetric power relationship. Honestly, the gap between the ideals I arrived with and the reality I've experienced is hard to overstate.

Q16.text: The psychological toll of feeling unseen as a thinker — reduced to a pair of hands rather than a developing scholar — is something I honestly didn't anticipate. And the stigma of leaving mid-candidature isn't something people talk about openly, which compounds the isolation considerably.

Q55.text: That supervisory fit — not departmental prestige or funding package — is the single variable that determines whether a PhD is survivable. I chose this program for all the wrong reasons.

Q41.text: Academic research or biomedical science — though I'm keeping science editing on the table, given what this experience has done to my appetite for institutional life.

Q60.text: The structural conditions that make bad supervision possible — opaque grievance processes, the taboo around speaking critically about supervisors while still enrolled, the way funding ties students to supervisors who have ceased to function as mentors — these deserve far more institutional attention than they receive. I hope this data is useful.

Q17.text: The intellectual challenge itself — when I'm actually allowed to think. That part hasn't disappointed me.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: In my lab, PhD students are expected to be completely independent with virtually no guidance or mentorship. I feel a worker, not like a student, and for this reason I think it's imperative we form works councils to protect our interests as doctoral candidates from opaque and arbitrary administrative decisions. The academic system appears to prize the publication of high impact papers over more intrinsic values, such as scientific merit, mentoring, and leadership abilities. Although PhD students work extremely hard, we get very little recognition. A high degree of work autonomy and the intellectual challenge of research are the main redeeming qualities, but sometimes fail to compensate for otherwise brutal conditions...

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a mixed bag -- there's real intellectual reward in the work itself, but the structure around it tends to normalize overwork and uncertainty in ways that feel kind of unnecessary. and I've come to see it less as a meritocracy and more as a system where persistence and luck matter in roughly equal measure, which I'm mostly at peace with.

Q16.text: The financial side of it, honestly -- like I went in knowing it wouldn't be lucrative but the gap between what a postdoc earns and what you need to actually live somewhere stable with decent benefits is kind of startling when you see it up close. it shapes a lot of my thinking about where this is all going.

Q55.text: That the timeline is basically fiction -- everyone talks about "finishing in four years" as if that's a real thing and not just a number on a funding form. I wish someone had told me early on that learning to sit with uncertainty and just keep working anyway is pretty much the whole skill, because I spent a lot of time in the first year waiting for things to feel more settled before I could really commit.

Q41.text: A stable research position at a university, ideally somewhere with decent benefits and job security -- I'm not chasing prestige at this point, I just want to do interesting work without the constant anxiety of short-term contracts.

Q60.text: Just that I appreciate surveys like this actually asking about the structural stuff and not just "how's your supervisor" -- there's a lot that goes unexamined in how PhD programs are designed and I think the more data researchers have on what the experience actually feels like from the inside, the better. I hope something useful comes out of it.

Q26.text: There are no incentives for professors to be excellent mentors. This is not because of any individual professor, but is a systemic issue. Universities hire professors based on their likeability, ability to carry out research, ability to acquire research funding, and ability to market their research in the form of publications, talks, and acclaim.

Q60.text: I think the relationship between industry and academia is perverse. Industry profits from public investment in academic research, and has no obligations to provide any societal benefit with those profits. National or non-profit labs should take academic research to the public. Public investment, public profits, societal benefits. The pharmaceutical industry is an exemplar of this relationship. Every drug has relied on public funding, yet no publicly funded patent returns those investments back into scientific grants. This change occurred during Reagan administration when patents became university rather than government grant office property.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it here, is honestly kind of stuck -- there are people doing genuinely interesting work, but the structures around them are outdated and I think actively prevent things from functioning well. My own situation involves spending a lot of time supporting other people's projects rather than developing my own research agenda, which is... fine in principle, except there's no real mechanism for accountability when that dynamic goes too far. I'm still committed to the actual science, but institutional culture leaves a lot to be desired.

Q16.text: The financial side of it, honestly -- PhD stipends in this context are not exactly generous, and when you factor in that you're essentially providing skilled labor (bioinformatics support is not trivial) for a rate that wouldn't survive comparison to any industry equivalent, it starts to feel less like a training opportunity and more like a structural arrangement that benefits everyone except the student. I don't want to be purely cynical about it, and I knew coming in that this wasn't going to be lucrative, but there's a difference between modest pay and feeling like the system is designed to extract work from people who have limited alternatives. And the mental load of that -- not just the workload itself but the awareness of it -- is something I didn't really anticipate.

Q55.text: That the supervisor relationship is more or less the whole thing -- not in the romantic "mentorship" sense, but structurally. Everything else (the project, the pace, whether you actually develop as researcher, whether you spend your time on your own work or propping up someone else's) flows downstream from that one dynamic, and you often don't have good information about it until you're already in it. I would have asked very different questions at the interview stage.

Q41.text: Applied bioinformatics in a medical or clinical setting -- hospital systems, diagnostics, or research institutes with an applied focus. I'm not particularly drawn to staying in academia, and the more time I spend here the more that feels like a reasonable conclusion rather than a failure. the actual work of analyzing genomic or clinical data in a context where it connects to patient outcomes is what interests me.

Q60.text: Something I didn't quite get to elsewhere -- I think the specific combination of being in a field like bioinformatics, where the skills are genuinely marketable outside academia, and being embedded in a system that doesn't fully acknowledge that, creates a particular kind of friction. You're aware the whole time that you could leave and be treated better, which makes the institutional dysfunction harder to just accept as "this is how it is." I dont know if that's relevant to what you're studying, but it felt worth saying.

Q17.text: The actual work -- the analysis, the moments when something in the data makes sense in a way you didn't expect. Bioinformatics has this quality where you're constantly sitting at the intersection of biological complexity and computational logic, and when those two things align it's genuinely satisfying in a way that's hard to replicate elsewhere. I also, maybe surprisingly given everything else, still enjoy the intellectual environment -- access to people who think carefully about hard problems is not nothing, even when the structural side of things is frustrating. It's not the totality of the experience, but it's enough to keep me here.

Q26.text: The system is built on hierarchy where junior researchers have almost no leverage, and the publish-or-perish pressure creates environment where misconduct is tolerated as long as output is high. I've witnessed things that would be actionable outside academia but get buried -- institutional self-protection, basically. Honestly it functions less like a meritocracy and more like feudal arrangement.

Q16.text: The dependency on supervisor references for future employment is a genuine structural vulnerability -- it effectively silences junior researchers who might otherwise report misconduct. I've had to start documenting everything in writing as precautionary measure, which honestly shouldn't be necessary. and the fact that this is just accepted as normal is probably the most concerning part.

Q55.text: That supervisors have almost unlimited informal power and very little accountability — I would have entered with written agreements on authorship and project scope from day one, not trusted goodwill.

Q41.text: Industry research is increasingly appealing -- academia's tolerance for misconduct makes it hard to see a future there, tbh. I'm keeping options open but with less idealism than I started with.

Q60.text: I hope this data is actually used to improve conditions for junior researchers -- surveys like this are only meaningful if institutions are willing to act on uncomfortable findings. Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it at ETH, functions reasonably well for those who are well-positioned within it — strong funding, intellectually engaged peers, and genuine research freedom are real advantages I don't take for granted. Kinda hard to evaluate the system fairly without holding both of those things at once.

Q16.text: The competitiveness of the academic job market is something I think about more than I anticipated — not with anxiety exactly, but honestly with a pragmatic awareness that tenure-track positions are scarce and the timelines are long. Q55.text: The importance of treating the PhD as a professional project with explicit milestones rather than an open-ended intellectual exploration — I wish I'd been more deliberate earlier about scoping work, setting deadlines, and having direct conversations with my supervisor about expectations on both sides.

Q26.text: Honestly, the academic system feels like it was built for people who dont need to worry about money, and that assumption runs pretty deep -- you're expected to treat financial precarity as something secondary to the work, which is easy to say when you dont have debt or family obligations waiting. the mentorship structures are weak and theres basically no accountability when supervisors fall short, so when things go wrong institutionally you're largely on your own to absorb it.

Q16.text: The mental health side of things, honestly -- there's a lot of ambient anxiety that I dont think anyone prepares you for, and the university's counseling resources are so stretched that by the time you get an appointment the acute moment has passed. and the way debt compounds while you're on a stipend that barely covers rent, it's kind of a constant background stress that makes it hard to just focus on the work the way everyone assumes you can.

Q55.text: That the stipend math doesnt actually work out the way you'd expect -- I knew it was low going in, but I didn't understand how it compounds against existing debt over years, and nobody walks you through that part before you sign anything. I wish I'd run the real numbers before committing, because the opportunity cost is significant and the institution doesnt factor any of that into its pitch to you

Q41.text: Something outside academia, pretty much entirely at this point. the financial reality of postdoc life -- more years of stipend-level pay with no job security -- just doesnt make sense given where I'm at with debt and family obligations. I'm looking at industry roles where the salary is predictable and the work-life balance is something you can actually negotiate for, rather than just accepting that your life is the PhD.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of data actually gets used to push for structural changes rather than just sit in a report somewhere -- the problems I've described aren't personal failures, theyre systemic, and the institution benefits from treating them as individual rather than collective. I don't expect much but I appreciated the chance to say it.

Q17.text: The intellectual side, genuinely -- when the research is actually going somewhere theres a kind of momentum that I dont get anywhere else, and for whatever its worth that part hasn't gone away even when everything else has felt like a grind. I just wish it existed in a context that didn't cost so much to sustain.

Q26.text: Because there are little to no metrics of evaluation for the PhD programme (none for evaluating PhD mentors, advisors etc) there is a lot of variability on how successful each student is and how terribly the PhD process can be. There is a lack of support of the students in many areas.

This is particularly worrisome because the interest rate does not go on hold while being a PhD student.

Q26.text: Broken incentives, mostly. The system rewards metrics over meaning -- impact factors, grant captures, citation counts -- and quietly punishes the slow careful basic research that actually builds knowledge. It's not unfixable, but you're not gonna fix it from the inside.

Q16.text: Peer review is genuinely broken -- reviewers incentivised to reject rather than engage, and the whole thing runs on unpaid labour anyway. And honestly the stipend situation is just embarrassing for an institution that relies this heavily on PhD students to keep the research running.

Q55.text: How political the whole enterprise is. Talent and rigor matter less than you think -- who your supervisor knows, which funding bodies are fashionable, whether your work fits the current grant cycle. I came in thinking good science would speak for itself. it doesn't, not reliably.

Q41.text: Science policy. I want to work on systemic reform -- funding structures, research priorities, how governments actually make decisions about science. Academia rewards individual output; policy is where you can change the rules of the game.

Q60.text: The peer review crisis and the basic research funding gap are both fixable problems -- we just lack the political will. Stop making scientists grovel for grants every two years and actually invest in foundational research. That's it, really.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Good things: intellectual freedom. Bad: Glorifying over working, low stipend, competing for grants is stressful, lack of work boundaries on weekends/during holidays, too much emphasis on applied and not basic research. If I could change one thing about academia, it would be to make universities do 70% basic and 30% applied research. The university is starting to look too much like industry- just let grad students do basic research and stop emphasizing man made metrics of success like impact factors and opportunities for application. The best applications often seem to come as by-products of people doing basic research (PCR, CRISPR, etc.). Stop making scientists grovel about their impact, just let them study nature.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Peer review needs to be more rigorous; initial screening for falsified data, re-used images, etc. The quality of our peer review determines the quality of our science and collective understanding. We need to revamp this- I am worried about how many poorly designed studies and misinterpretation of results are published, and how it is clouding our body of knowledge and leading us down fields and research paths that just aren't real or true. We need a generation that is more discerning and doesn't just trust something because it is published; in that sense, I'm worried about the state and fate of science.

Q26.text: Structurally, the system seems designed for a world that no longer exists -- faculty positions as the default outcome, four-year timelines as realistic, institutions as inherently supportive. The intellectual community is genuinely one of the better parts of the experience. But institutional support, especially for students in newer programs without established norms to lean on, is pretty thin, and the gap between what's implied at recruitment and what you actually encounter is hard to overlook.

Q16.text: The timeline is a real concern -- I'm increasingly skeptical that four years is achievable, partly because being the first student through the program means I've had to lay administrative groundwork that later students won't need to. And honestly, the career side of things is harder to sit with than I expected. Government hiring has become pretty unpredictable, and I'm not sure how much of that is cyclical versus structural

Q55.text: That institutional infrastructure matters as much as intellectual fit. I spent a lot of the first year navigating things -- committee structures, milestone timelines, administrative pathways -- that more established programs have already worked out. Knowing that upfront would have changed how I evaluated programs, and honestly might have changed the decision.

Q41.text: Government policy or analysis roles are my first preference, though the hiring environment rn makes it hard to count on that. Consulting is a realistic fallback, and I haven't ruled out academia -- I may also be interested in research-facing roles that sit at the intersection of methods and applied work -- but it's not the primary goal.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of data gets used in ways that actually reach decision-makers -- the structural issues aren't subtle, and I don't think individual resilience is the right frame for solving them. The students who struggle aren't struggling because they're underprepared; the programs just weren't built with them in mind. Anyway, thanks for putting this together.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual community is the clearest answer -- conversations with people who are genuinely invested in ideas, across departments, are pretty rare outside academia and I don't take that for granted. There's also something I find satisfying about working on problems with actual methodological depth, even when the structural conditions around that work are frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There isn't a lot of sympathy for students going through the process. Advisers and mentors have the mindset of "well I did it, so you should be able to do it too" in regards to work-life balance, low income, and general stress levels. They don't consider what going through the system has done to them or whether it impacted them negatively. In addition, many advisers have chosen to enter academia; therefore, their career advice is generally targeted to that area.

Q26.text: The academic system is structurally broken in ways that aren't accidental -- they're baked in. It rewards a very narrow kind of productivity while systematically ignoring the financial realities facing graduate students. The mentorship model is essentially a lottery: you either get a good PI or you don't, and there's no real accountability when you don't. I genuinely love the intellectual environment of a university. But the machinery around it? It needs to be rebuilt, not patched.

Q16.text: The financial piece keeps me up at night more than I expected when I started. I knew stipends were low -- I didn't account for what it would actually mean to watch peers in industry triple their income while I'm still deferring loans and postponing basic life decisions. Starting a family, buying a house, those feel genuinely out of reach right now. and the late-stage isolation hits harder than anyone talks about. Nobody warns you how untethered it gets when you're years in, your PI is checked out, and you're seriously questioning whether any of it was worth the opportunity cost.

Q55.text: That the relationship with your PI is essentially the whole ballgame -- and you have almost no way to evaluate it before you commit. I knew it mattered. I didn't understand that a checked-out supervisor doesn't just slow you down, it fundamentally changes what your PhD *is*. You're not getting mentored, you're freelancing with a stipend. If I could go back, I'd spend way more time talking to current students, not faculty, before I signed anything.

Q41.text: Management consulting is the primary target, honestly -- I want to apply the analytical skills without being trapped in the academic incentive structure. Executive recruiting is also on the table; understanding how institutions work feels relevant there. Policy is a longer shot but I find myself drawn to it given how much I think about systemic reform in higher education. Academia is essentially off the table at this point.

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone actually reads these. There's a pattern in what PhD students are saying -- financially stressed, poorly mentored, actively leaving -- and it keeps getting treated as individual failure rather than systemic output. It's not. The incentive structures produce exactly this result, predictably, at scale. If universities are serious about retaining talent and not just extracting it, the reforms have to go deeper than wellness workshops and "mental health days." Stipends need to reflect actual cost of living. PIs need accountability mechanisms that have teeth. and students need real career support that doesn't treat anything outside tenure-track as a consolation prize. I'm one data point, but I doubt I'm an outlier.

Q17.text: The intellectual environment, genuinely. Being surrounded by people who care deeply about ideas -- even when the institution is failing them -- is something I don't take for granted. The library access, the seminars, the weird niche conversations that happen at 2pm on a random Tuesday. Honestly, it's the one part I'm not ready to let go of. The actual science still pulls me. It's everything built around it that's broken.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Broken. The wages are skewed. The incentives for faculty to publish in high impact factor journals make graduate students not have as many publications. There's fierce competition for grants which incentivizes cheating. The goal for the graduate student is to graduate and find employment but the goal for the faculty is to produce research and papers, thus these are at conflict. As a grad student becomes well trained, the faculty don't want to let them graduate because they have cheap, well trained, labor. Academic postdoc positions are the same. They're lowly paid but highly competent individuals. Faculty in universities still aren't aware of the data regarding competition for new faculty positions (despite serving on search panels). The whole system is broken.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The biggest, most overwhelming concern for the entirety of my PhD is trying to find good employment afterwards that can cover my student debt and allow me to start a family. Unfortunately, academic postdoc positions in the US do not pay enough to do this, which means I have to find a non-default path.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Good science and good management/leadership do not overlap. My PI is a great scientist but he is a TERRIBLE manager. This is likely why the average time to degree for my lab is 8 years when the department average is 6.5. He's incredibly hands off, provides no positive feedback, and discourages many things. You have to fight tooth and nail to get what you want unless you're his favorite student.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: One that intersects with the life sciences but doesn't require bench research. I'd be happy continuing computational (genomic) research. I enjoy meetings and administrative/leadership/management work. Perhaps a policy analyst and strategy position. I'm currently targeting management consulting, executive recruiting, and policy analyst positions for application.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: We don't have an excess of people with PhD degrees. The world needs more highly educated people. We have a broken system that provides incentive for poor quality of life for graduate students and postdocs -- low pay, aggressive competition, long hours, discouragement from leaving the academic environment. This can be fixed, but it needs to be a top-down move away from the publish or perish environment. Even more faculty positions aren't necessary. Staff research positions would be great. Tenure-track teaching positions (divide the labor so some faculty are almost full time research, many are teaching) would make a significant difference. Put hard caps on graduate programs (6 years) to force program progression. Many people in my program don't defend their prospectus until year 5 which is COMPLETELY inappropriate. There is no department or university recourse for this.

Q26.text: Broken, honestly. It's a system designed for a world that no longer exists -- where faculty positions were plentiful and a PhD actually meant career security. Q16.text: The stipend thing just doesn't get talked about enough. I'm in year 5, I have a master's degree's worth of expertise at this point, and I'm making less than a first-year teacher. Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. As a department we also regularly experience what we perceive as discrimination from reviewers towards third world universities, even when the results are objectively valuable and can be quickly reproduced with no effort (such as running a script with fully free and open source code). Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. The quality of your research is largely irrelevant, even in fields where problems have objective and established metrics for the quality of solutions.

Q26.text: The academic system is structurally broken in ways that are hard to ignore once you're inside it. It relies on the idea that doing a PhD is calling, not a job, and uses that framing to justify paying people below living wage, normalizing 60-hour weeks, treating instability as character-building. I had my PI change partway through, had to restart essentially from scratch -- and the system treats that as just... part of the deal. Honestly it's not. The labor conditions in academia would not be acceptable in any other skilled profession, and the fact that we accept them says more about how effectively the passion narrative has been weaponized than about genuine love of research. I do love the research, that's separate. But the system surrounding it needs structural reform, not just better supervisors.

Q16.text: The financial side is honestly the thing that weighs on me most day-to-day. The stipend doesn't cover cost of living in a German city, and the unspoken expectation is that you should be grateful regardless. And there's a kind of isolation that accumulates over time -- not just social, but intellectual, because almost no one outside academia understands what the work actually involves or what the stakes are. I also worry about the precarity of what comes after. Even if I do everything right, the pipeline into stable research positions is so narrow that it's hard not to feel like the whole thing is a gamble I've already committed to.

Q55.text: That you should treat choosing a supervisor like choosing business partner, not a mentor. I came in thinking the relationship would be mostly about intellectual guidance. it's not -- it's a power relationship, and if it breaks down, you are the one who absorbs the cost. I restarted two years in after a PI change, and there's essentially no structural protection when that happens. No one warned me that was even a real possibility, let alone how to vet for it.

Q41.text: Science communication, with a foot still in research if I can manage it. I want to do work that actually reaches people outside the academic bubble -- writing, public engagement, maybe policy-adjacent stuff. I'm not interested in the traditional tenure-track path, tbh. The pipeline is too narrow and the labor conditions aren't worth it for me personally.

Q60.text: Just want to say that surveys like this matter -- if the data actually goes somewhere and informs how institutions think about PhD conditions, that's worth something. I'm skeptical that much will change structurally, but I'd rather participate and be wrong than disengage. The issues I've described aren't personal grievances, they're systemic, and the more data exists on how widespread they are the harder it becomes to dismiss them as individual cases of people who just couldn't hack it.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly. Getting to spend time on a problem that actually matters to me, going deep on something most people never engage with -- that part is real and I don't want to understate it. There's also something to be said for the community of people who take ideas seriously, even if the structural conditions around that community are pretty frustrating most of the time.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system right now is outdated and based on the notion we should work because we are lucky to be doing our hobbies. my PhD should not be seen as an hobby but as a normal job and entitled to the same benefits/rules as a normal job

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The lack of respect for my job as a PhD student from the academy, some of my peers and society in general. My PhD is a job, I work full time on it and however I am only payed 50% (in Germany) of my salary because I am "student". When I complain that this is unfair, that I am not being payed for my full work hours or my extra hours (that are always expected of me as a PhD student); I am told that 1) I should be grateful for even getting paid, other disciplines are not 2) I benefit from student discounts so I should not complain for receiving less (I would happily give away my student discounts if I was payed a full salary!) 3) I should be happy because I am doing my passion job (passion is not going to feed me in my retirement). Not being entitle to a full salary, extra hours or even a contract that will allow us to receive some help after our working years is destroying our future before it even starts.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I did not start my PhD directly after the masters, I was working sometime as a research assistant. So by the time I decided to do a PhD I knew exactly why I was doing it and what were some of the possible challenges. As such I was prepared to keep going despite having to change my first PI (due to PI sickness) and restarting my PhD after 2 years and despite having a new PI now that is not meeting my expectations. So, I do think i was prepared to do a PhD when I started. Personally, from what I see around me, I would just tell everyone to not do a PhD right after the master/bachelor but to take their time and to find if a PhD is really what they want to do.

Q26.text: Universities need better financing. There are not enough opportunities to get employed after the PhD. There is a huge uncertainty. Most of PhD students I know work very hard and are poorly paid, often handed even responsibilities they are not supposed to take care of. Over 12 hours a day in a lab are not an exception. I am lucky enough to have a great supervisor with reasonable demands, who even gives me freedom in research and supports my creativity. I believe that it is not about the system, but the individuals in it. I think our academic system has approved in the recent years and that PhD student get more support, but most of the problems can't be easily solved by other system changes. As long as PhD students are viewed by most as a cheap workforce to exploit, instead of young scientists with bright ideas and hopeful future, the academia can't move much further.

Q26.text: The system is supportive in some ways — my institution has decent resources and my supervisor is reasonable — but it's also kind of designed to isolate you. Q26.text: The academic system has genuine intellectual merit and I remain committed to the research itself, but the structural realities -- underfunding, lab overcrowding, and the kind of administrative opacity that leaves students in limbo for months -- create enormous friction that seems almost by design, and what I've found most disheartening, honestly, is that institutional dysfunction is rarely acknowledged as a systemic problem but is instead treated as something individual researchers simply need to navigate on their own, which places an unreasonable burden on those who entered in good faith with serious long-term commitments. It's exhausting.

Q16.text: The mental and emotional toll, honestly, is something I hadn't fully anticipated -- not just the stress of the research itself, but the cumulative weight of sensing that the institution isn't particularly invested in your success, and given my age and the professional years I've set aside to do this, there's an ongoing anxiety about whether what I've sacrificed will actually translate into something viable in neuroscience research. that's not something you can simply reason your way past.

Q55.text: How genuinely opaque the internal politics of lab allocation and funding are, and how little of that is ever communicated to incoming students -- I was given every assurance that the lab I needed would be accessible, and it wasn't, and by the time that became clear I was already committed in ways that weren't easy to undo. I wish someone had told me plainly that institutional promises and institutional capacity are not the same thing.

Q41.text: Neuroscience research, ideally in a capacity that draws on my background in microbiology, statistics, and psychology -- I came to this degree with a specific integrative vision and that hasn't changed, though I'll admit the institutional experience has made me think more carefully about what kind of environment I'd actually want to work in afterward.

Q60.text: I hope the data collected here is actually used to inform structural change rather than simply producing reports that get filed and forgotten, because the problems I've described -- the funding gaps, the lab access issues, the administrative opacity -- aren't unique to me and I'd be surprised if I'm the only respondent raising them. I came into this degree with significant professional experience and what I'd characterize as realistic expectations, and I've still found the gap between what institutions promise and what they deliver to be larger than I anticipated. I don't want to end on a purely critical note because the research itself remains genuinely meaningful to me and I have good working relationships with people across the labs I've ended up spanning, but I do think universities have a responsibility to be more honest with mature-age students in particular about the resource constraints they'll actually face, rather than letting people make major life decisions on the basis of assurances that aren't backed by capacity. that's the main thing I'd want decision-makers to take away.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue genuinely integrative questions -- bringing microbiology, statistics, and psychology into conversation with neuroscience in ways that wouldn't have been possible in any of my previous roles -- that's the part that still feels worthwhile, and honestly it's what keeps me going on the days when the institutional side of things is most draining. There's a real satisfaction in the research itself that I don't want to lose sight of, even when everything around it is difficult.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Lack of funding and PhD students converting from full time to part time officially but actually working full time so they can get through the experimental workload has crowded out my preferred lab choice & I could not get a position due to lack of funding and overcrowding. I am now trying to do the same research under neuroscience and link into different labs as I design an experiment. The benefit is I am not tied to any one lab but it increases the stress around the experimental stages of my degree due to not gaining access to a lab or failing to get funding. I was very disappointed by the faculty allowing students to be enrolled part time but work full time as this also was not reflected in lab availability as well as very costly in lab equipment and consumables being used at a full time rate rather than a part time rate which drained the lab budget causing the lab to almost run out of money and engage in talks of letting go of the post docs because of funding issues around ability to pay them.

This gave me a great deal of concern even though I was later told this issues had nothing to do with me, my abilities or qualifications.

Q26.text: Hierarchical, opaque, and largely indifferent to the people inside it. power concentrated, accountability rampant in name only, rhetoric of mentorship masking cold-blooded gatekeeping. I came in believing in knowledge; I found credentialing machine, honestly.

Q55.text: That the politics matter more than the work. Supervisor selection is career-determining in ways no one explains -- not talent, not output, proximity to right power broker. I optimized for intellectual fit; should have mapped the department's fault lines first, honestly.
