Q26.text: The academic system has real intellectual merit but is structurally dependent on supervisory relationships that lack adequate accountability mechanisms. When that relationship fails, there are few formal recourse options, and publication progress stalls -- with lasting consequences for career trajectory. It functions well for those with attentive supervision; for others, it can be professionally costly in ways the institution doesn't fully acknowledge.

Q16.text: The absence of formal midpoint reviews or progress audits genuinely concerns me -- there's no institutional checkpoint that would have flagged supervisory disengagement early enough to matter. by the time issues become visible, the damage to publication timelines is already done and hard to recover from.

Q55.text: That supervisory fit matters as much as institutional prestige -- probably more. I prioritised the lab's research profile when choosing supervisor and gave little weight to their actual availability or mentorship track record, which I'd weigh very differently now

Q41.text: Independent research, ideally outside of a clinical-academic setting, or a role in science communication -- writing, editing, policy-adjacent work. Honestly the publication barriers I've encountered have made me less certain that a conventional academic path is realistic or even desirable rn.

Q60.text: The structural issues I've described aren't unique to my situation -- I've spoken with peers in similar programs who've had comparable experiences with clinician-supervisors whose clinical commitments simply don't leave room for adequate PhD oversight. It might be worth the institution examining whether the current supervisory model is fit for purpose in biomedical programs where supervisors carry heavy clinical loads. Honest accountability structures -- not just end-of-candidature reviews -- could make a real difference.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue a specific research question in depth is genuinely rewarding -- there's a quality of sustained focus that's hard to find in other roles. I also value the collegial environment, though honestly that's been more product of peer relationships than formal structures.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a system designed to extract labor from people at their most vulnerable and call it intellectual development. The power dynamics are pretty ruthless -- advisors hold enormous leverage over students whose careers depend entirely on their goodwill, and there's very little structural accountability for how that power gets used. I've come to see the degree as a credential to survive rather than a process that truly works for the people going through it

Q16.text: The financial precarity is something I think about more than I expected -- the stipend barely covers rent, and watching peers in industry earn three times as much for fewer hours and far less psychological stress makes it hard to maintain any illusion that this is worth it on material terms. And honestly, the mental health toll is real; there's a kind of chronic low-grade anxiety that I don't think I had before, and I'm not sure it fully goes away even after you leave.

Q55.text: That advisor selection is everything, and the institutional signals you're given to evaluate them — publication count, grant funding, departmental reputation — are almost entirely uncorrelated with whether they'll treat you like a person rather than a resource. I picked someone who looked excellent on paper, and I've spent years managing the consequences of that.

Q41.text: Data science or analytics in industry, or failing that, high school teaching. Honestly I'd take the pay cut for teaching over staying in academia -- the idea of a job with actual boundaries and some respect for your time sounds almost foreign to me at this point.

Q60.text: The system runs on the assumption that people will keep absorbing the costs -- psychological, financial, professional -- because they've invested too much to walk away. And for a long time that worked on me too. But I think the most clarifying thing about reaching the end of a PhD is that you stop being afraid of the sunk cost and start doing the math on what you're actually getting versus what you're giving up. For most people I know, that math doesn't work out. I genuinely hope whoever reads this uses it for something -- if there's a way to make these programs less extractive, that would matter more than another incremental publication in a journal nobody reads.

Q17.text: The intellectual problem itself, when I can actually get to it -- there are moments where the work is genuinely interesting and I remember why I started. But those moments are pretty rare, and they're getting harder to access when so much of the time is spent navigating the politics around the work rather than doing it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I have a very dismal view of the academic system in general. The majority of my work has almost nothing to do with "education" and instead is truly work being done for my professor that has very little chance of benefiting me or advancing my career independently. In the resource constrained environment of University research, I understand the structural advantage of using a large army of underpaid/overworked graduate students to slog through the work, but the system seems to avoid any sense of good management or efficient work/support. The majority of my time is wasted, but because my time is so inexpensive, this is viewed as acceptable.

Q55.text: Remember that I am here for purely self-motivated reasons. If there is an obstacle from my department or advisor, do not go along with it. Be absolutely ruthless towards the interests of others in order to graduate as quickly as possible.

Q26.text: Fundamentally broken in ways that are structural, not incidental. The attitude from faculty/PIs that students are a renewable resource to be worked until they break, the expectation that passion should substitute for adequate compensation, the institutional indifference to mental health until it becomes a liability -- these arent individual failures, they're features of a system designed to extract labor cheaply. I came in genuinely committed to research and I'm leaving with a body that's carried the cost of that commitment.

Q16.text: The financial precarity, honestly -- watching colleagues quietly take on debt or second jobs just to stay enrolled while PIs publish on their work. And the normalization of it, the way you're made to feel grateful for the stipend rather than underpaid for the labor. I've also had real concerns about how little recourse exists when a supervisor relationship deteriorates; the power asymmetry makes formal complaints functionally useless for most people.

Q55.text: That the supervisor relationship is essentially unbreakable once you're in it -- the power differential means you can't leave without career consequences, and departments have every incentive to protect the PI over the student. I would have vetted mine so much more carefully, talked to former students, looked for patterns rather than taking the lab visit at face value. knowing that going in wouldn't have fixed the system but it might have saved me a few years of diminishing returns and a lot of physical health I can't get back.

Q41.text: Industry — specifically pharmaceutical clinical outcomes research. After four years of watching academic institutions treat their graduate students as disposable labor, I have no interest in perpetuating that system. the pay is better, the hours have some semblance of boundaries, and the work is applied in ways that actually reach patients rather than sitting behind journal paywalls.

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone reads these responses and takes them seriously rather than aggregating them into a report that gets shelved. The problems I've described aren't edge cases -- they're the median experience for PhD students in underfunded programs with asymmetric power structures. if there's any policy lever being considered here, prioritize independent ombudsperson structures and stipend floors that aren't contingent on supervisor goodwill. The goodwill model has failed pretty comprehensively.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual freedom -- or what was left of it before grant pressures and PI expectations colonized even that. There are moments, fewer now than four years ago, where the work itself is genuinely interesting. but it's hard to enjoy much when your health is paying the tab.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Needs major reform. There should be standards for living and mental health that all programs across fields should be required to abide by. There should also be annual training for faculty (regardless of tenure/career level) on how to mentor students.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: It's genuinely good at producing knowledge, I think, but pretty indifferent to people doing the producing. There's a lot of infrastructure for research outputs -- publications, grants, metrics -- and comparatively little attention to whether students are actually okay. And the gap between what we do in the lab and what the public understands feels like it's not really anyone's official job to fix, which is kind of a systemic failure honestly

Q16.text: Mental health is something I think about more than I expected to, honestly. Not in a crisis way, but the low-level uncertainty -- whether you're progressing fast enough, whether the work will actually matter outside the lab -- it kind of accumulates over time. I also worry about isolation, especially when your research feels pretty niche and there aren't many people around who can even follow what you're doing. And the career piece is still unresolved for me; I'm open to different directions but that openness can feel more like floating than freedom sometimes

Q55.text: That the uncertainty doesn't really go away -- I assumed it was just beginning stage and that once I got further into the work things would feel more settled. but the ambiguity is kind of structural, not a phase you move through. Q41.text: Honestly, I'm still figuring that out -- which I know isn't a very satisfying answer. Q60.text: Just that I hope surveys like this actually get read by people with some ability to act on them -- that's not a dig, I genuinely don't know what happens to the data and I guess I'm curious. There is a lack of support for personal developments, or even interests in non-academic careers, from the department of chemistry at my school.

Q26.text: Honestly, competitive is the first word that comes to mind. Everyone's racing to publish, racing to get grants, guarding their work like it's a trade secret — there's very little sense of shared purpose. I came in hoping for real collaboration, for community, and what I found was more like parallel isolation instead. People physically in the same building and still not really working together. It's kind of exhausting, and I keep wondering if this is just how it is everywhere or if it doesn't have to be this way.

Q16.text: The mental health side of things, honestly. I wasn't prepared for how lonely it would feel day to day, and I don't think the department really acknowledges that. there's no real structure for building connection between students — no communal space that actually gets used, no culture of checking in on each other. It's like everyone's expected to just figure it out alone, and that's been harder than the research itself at times.

Q55.text: That doing a PhD is fundamentally a solo endeavour in most places, no matter what the department website says about "vibrant research communities." I wish someone had told me upfront that I'd need to build my own support network outside the department — because waiting for it to emerge naturally just doesn't work, and I wasted a lot of time feeling like something was wrong with me when really it's just how academia is set up.

Q41.text: Teaching and outreach, primarily. I want to work somewhere that actually values connection — students, public engagement, maybe some community-facing research. I'm not ruling out research entirely but honestly the idea of being stuck in the publish-or-perish cycle doesn't appeal to me at all rn. Something in higher ed teaching or science communication feels more like where I want to be.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this data actually gets used to make things better, not just filed away. The isolation issue is real and it doesn't get talked about enough. Academia keeps recruiting people who value community and then offering them the opposite — and then acting surprised when retention is a problem. I dont have a neat solution but I do think even small structural changes, like actual shared spaces that get used, or peer support built into the program, would make a difference. thanks for asking.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, if I'm being honest. I get to spend my days actually thinking deeply about something I care about, and that part — when it's working — is genuinely good. There's also something I value about the flexibility, even if it comes with its own stress. But it's kind of hard to separate the enjoyment from everything else that comes with it. most days the isolation undercuts it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I can repeat what I wrote above. I think there is too much time alone. I had expected to become part of a creative and established research group, but there is basicaly no group. Everyone is occupied with their own businesses. There is also no proper introduction for phd-students at the department and you are left alone to figure out where to go and what to do. And that you are trained to think egoistic and not collaborative is not constructive! At least not to me.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The unhealthy egoistic culture in academia. I think high-quality research evolves from smart people working together thinking out solutions together, however, the competitiveness between researchers and the little available funding destroy this possibility. I think it is an unhealthy culture to be part of. Furthermore, publications in high-impact journals are valued more than for instance teaching experience and ability when you apply for permanent positions. I think society looses a lot on this, as we end up with a lot of (again) egoistic people at the universities, who then is forced to teach, but feel that it is a waste of time and the result is low-quality teaching.

Q55.text: That my main-advisor is not a group person but works better individually, which is completely opposite of me. That both my main supervisors always travel and very seldom are present at the department (contributing to even less research group feeling).

Q26.text: Bloated and self-perpetuating, tbh. The whole thing feels like it was designed to reproduce more academics rather than solve actual problems -- and most of the coursework is just hoops to jump through. I genuinely cant see how half of what I've done maps to anything useful in industry or government research. it rewards playing the game, not doing good work.

Q16.text: The opportunity cost keeps me up at night more than anything else. Every year I'm in here is a year I'm not building real skills, not earning a real salary, not doing work that actually ships or matters. My friends who went straight to industry are two promotions ahead of me and I'm sitting here debugging simulation code that maybe three people will ever read. And honestly the isolation is brutal -- you're supposed to be "part of a research community" but in practice it's just you and your desk and a supervisor who checks in when it's convenient for them. That's the thing nobody warns you about.

Q55.text: That the timeline is a fiction. Everyone says "three to four years" like it's a real number, and it's not -- it's a best-case marketing figure that assumes nothing goes wrong, your supervisor is engaged, and your project doesn't pivot halfway through. I wish someone had just been straight with me about the actual distribution of outcomes before I signed up.

Q41.text: Industry research or government research. I want to do work that actually gets used -- not papers that sit behind a paywall and get cited twice.

Q60.text: The whole experience has made me pretty cynical about the value proposition of a PhD, at least in my field. If I could go back I'd seriously consider skipping straight to industry and trying to find a research role there -- the skills gap honestly isn't as big as academia wants you to believe. The credential might open some doors but I'm not sure it's worth three-to-five years of your life and the salary hit. hope whoever reads this actually does something with it rather than filing it away.

Q17.text: Honestly? The autonomy, when it actually exists. There are stretches where I get to just dig into a problem without anyone telling me how to do it, and that part's genuinely good. But it's hard to enjoy even that when you're aware the whole time that the problem might not matter to anyone outside this building.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It is not beneficial for people who want to start working and actually do something. Also not beneficial for entrepreneurial pursuits and multidisciplinary collaboration. It is isolated and particular. Thus, depending on what you study you will either have great skills to market to industry prospects or none at all.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: What the hell is the point? You do your four years in undergraduate studies and then start graduate studies. Your professors are usually just as mediocre as your undergraduate professors and you have to complete this core curriculum which is just undergraduate extended. So, not only did you have to work your butt off for four years and then complete graduate examinations. But then, you have to repeat the process for about 1.5 years in graduate school. THEN you're completely free to do research. But, you have about 3 years to become sufficiently good enough to contribute. You do this and that only to write a dissertation about an esoteric topic that nobody else will ever care about. Meanwhile, people who didn't do graduate school have been in the workplace this entire time working and gaining experience doing real-world work. You get this degree to work in the world without ever learning how to. Graduate school is mostly a sham.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it, is structured to protect institutional interests above individual ones -- supervisors weather burnout with minimal accountability while students absorb the consequences. Promises about projects and funding evaporate when political obstacles arise, and the blame quietly redistributes downward. its a system I'm honestly relieved to be leaving.

Q16.text: The erosion of the original project scope has been a persistent concern — the grant work that initially drew me to this program simply never happened, and no one in the department has been willing to acknowledge that as a systemic failure rather than a personal one. I've also found the isolation harder than expected; when the supervisory relationship breaks down, there's very little structural support to fill that gap, and asking for help can feel like it will be used against you later.

Q55.text: How little recourse you actually have when supervisory relationship fails. I came in assuming there would be formal mechanisms if something went seriously wrong -- escalation paths, mediation, intervention -- but honestly the institution's first instinct is to protect itself, not the student. Knowing that going in would have changed how I documented everything from day one.

Q41.text: Data science outside academia, ideally in industry where deliverables are actually defined and accountability runs in both directions. I've spent enough time in an environment where promises dissolve and blame flows downward -- I'm not gonna carry that forward into my career if I can help it.

Q60.text: I hope the data from surveys like this actually feeds back into policy in some meaningful way -- the supervisory accountability gap isn't an edge case, its a structural feature. Students don't report problems because the systems designed to help them are the same ones that will quietly hold it against them. I'm not optimistic that changes quickly, but I'd rather have said it than not.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least from what I have seen here in Czech Republic and in Brazil, feels increasingly driven by a logic of pure productivity -- publish more, produce faster, fill databases with papers that sometimes say very little. I find it troubling that young researchers are pushed to execute technical work without really stopping to think if the hypothesis they are testing is even worth pursuing in the first place. For me, science was always about asking the right questions before answering them. but this culture rewards the quantity of answers, not the quality of the inquiry. I still love science, honestly, but I'm worried we are turning researchers into technicians.

Q16.text: One thing that concerns me a lot, and that I did not expect before starting, is the isolation. Not social isolation exactly, but intellectual isolation — the feeling that there is no real space to discuss ideas, to question whether what we are doing actually makes sense. People are always busy with their own projects, their own deadlines, and conversation about the deeper purpose of the research is kind of... absent. I come from philosophy background before moving to science, so maybe I am more sensitive to this, but I genuinely miss the culture of argumentation. And honestly, I worry sometimes that I am adapting to a system I think is wrong, just because the pressure to publish is so constant. that is maybe the concern that weighs on me the most.

Q55.text: I wish I had known that choosing where to do the PhD is as important — maybe more important — than the research topic itself. I chose my current program for the scientific opportunity, and I do not regret that entirely, but I underestimated how much the intellectual culture of a place would shape my experience. If I could go back, I would ask: is there space here to think, to argue, to question the premises of the work? Not just, is there funding, is there good laboratory. The science you can learn anywhere, honestly. But if you land in an environment where ideas are not taken seriously, you spend years doing work without really understanding why it matters — and that, I think, is kind of a quiet damage that is hard to recover from.

Q41.text: I want to lead my own research group in oncology -- that is the main goal. I am also genuinely interested in science communication, because I think one of the problems with academia is that researchers dont talk to the public about why their work matters. so maybe some combination of both.

Q60.text:
I want to say thank you for creating space for this kind of reflection, because I think surveys like this one matter -- not just as data collection, but as a small act of acknowledgment that the PhD experience is complex and that researchers are people, not just output machines. I hope the results are used to actually improve the system, and not just to describe it. That distinction, between diagnosing and changing, is one I think about a lot in my own work. If there is anyone reading these answers who has influence over how doctoral programs are designed, I would ask them to take seriously the question of intellectual culture, not just infrastructure or funding. A laboratory with good equipment but no space for genuine argument is, in my opinion, a wasted opportunity.

Pedro Zeni

Q17.text: Honestly, what I enjoy most is the moments -- and they are not always frequent -- when I am genuinely thinking. Not executing, not producing, but actually wrestling with a problem that I find beautiful or difficult or both. There is something in the act of reading a paper and feeling that I have something to argue against, or talking with someone who pushes me to sharpen an idea. those moments remind me why I came here in the first place. I also enjoy the freedom, the fact that I am, in principle, responsible for my own intellectual trajectory, even if the system sometimes makes that feel more theoretical than real.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Espero que o fruto do meu PhD consiga atingir este objetivo.

Q26.text: The system, honestly, rewards visibility over substance -- publications, grants, and conference presence count for more than the quality or originality of the work itself. I came in with genuine intellectual curiosity but its become clear that career advancement depends as much on self-promotion and the right institutional connections as on anything you actually produce. Q16.text: The job market is probably what weighs on me most rn, honestly. The number of permanent academic positions relative to the PhDs being produced simply doesn't add up, and my supervisor -- who secured their position in a very different era -- seems genuinely unable to grasp that its a structural problem rather than a personal failing

Q55.text: That the skills you develop during a PhD -- the analytical rigour, the ability to design experiments, synthesise literature, manage ambiguous problems -- are genuinely valued outside academia. I spent a long time assuming the only legitimate outcome was a postdoc, and that framing caused a lot of unnecessary anxiety. Knowing earlier that science-adjacent roles in industry or policy weren't a consolation prize would have changed how I thought about the whole process

Q41.text: Science-adjacent roles outside academia -- policy, research translation, or industry R&D are all things I'm looking at seriously. I'm not ruling academia out entirely but the structural realities I've encountered make it hard to plan around a career path that depends so heavily on luck and timing

Q60.text: I'd just add that surveys like this matter -- not because they'll change incentive structures overnight, but because the PhD experience is systematically underdocumented relative to the rhetoric about "training the next generation." The gap between what the system promises and what it delivers is real, and honestly I hope the data here is actually used somewhere it can have effect

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom -- when you actually have it -- is genuinely something I value. There's still a version of this life where you spend your days reading deeply, designing experiments, and working through problems that don't have obvious answers, and that part hasn't entirely disappeared for me. it's just that it exists alongside enough structural frustration that it's hard to appreciate without qualification.
